blocks.content: docker logs shows you what a container's main process has printed to standard output and standard error, since it started. It is usually the very first thing you check when a container is misbehaving.
1. Docker Captures stdout and stderr Automatically
blocks.text: 1. Docker Captures stdout and stderr Automatically

blocks.content: You never have to configure anything for this to work, Docker automatically captures everything a container's main process writes to stdout and stderr, and docker logs simply reads that captured stream back.

blocks.alt: Everything printed by the main process is captured automatically

blocks.content:
docker logs web
# Prints everything the "web" container has output
# since it started, oldest first.

code.content:
docker logs web
# Prints everything the "web" container has output
# since it started, oldest first.

codes.bash:
docker logs web
# Prints everything the "web" container has output
# since it started, oldest first.

blocks.content: Adding -f (follow) keeps the command running and streams new log lines as they are written, exactly like tail -f on a regular log file. This is the standard way to watch a container's behavior in real time while you reproduce an issue.

blocks.alt: Follow mode streams new lines as they happen

blocks.content:
docker logs -f web
# Stays attached, printing new lines as the container
# produces them, until you Ctrl+C.

code.content:
docker logs -f web
# Stays attached, printing new lines as the container
# produces them, until you Ctrl+C.

codes.bash:
docker logs -f web
# Stays attached, printing new lines as the container
# produces them, until you Ctrl+C.

blocks.content: 3. Only the Main Process Is Captured
blocks.text: 3. Only the Main Process Is Captured

blocks.content: It is worth being precise here: docker logs only ever shows output from the container's main process (PID 1). Anything printed by a separate docker exec session you opened into that same container does not appear in docker logs at all, since it was never part of the captured stream.

blocks.alt: Only the main process feeds into docker logs

blocks.title: Key Takeaway
points: docker logs reads the stdout/stderr Docker has been capturing from a container's main process since it started, no extra setup required.
Only the main process (PID 1) feeds docker logs, output from a docker exec session into the same container is invisible to it.
